\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Functionally equivalent register-transfer-level (RTL) modules can differ
sharply in achievable clock frequency.  We train an RTL generator with a
correctness-gated physical objective: an input/output-equivalence oracle rejects
incorrect modules before a learned frequency proxy supplies reward.  The proxy
guides training but never supplies an evaluation result.  Instead, evaluation
joins original sample multiplicities to real post-route Vivado measurements and
assigns zero frequency to incorrect and implementation-failed samples.  On a
split frozen before policy training, spanning \claim{DesignCount} designs and
\claim{FamilyCount} accelerator families, this equal-sample endpoint rises from
\claim{OverallSftPenalized} to \claim{OverallGrpoPenalized}~MHz and improves on
\claim{OverallImproved} designs.  The paired gains are
\claim{InterpGain}~MHz under interpolation and \claim{ExtrapGain}~MHz under
extrapolation.  A second code-model backbone replicates the result on an earlier
\claim{QwenDesignCount}-design split: \claim{QwenOverallSftPenalized} to
\claim{QwenOverallGrpoPenalized}~MHz, with every evaluated design improving.
Candidate-level measurements explain the shift: the mean probability on the
most frequent distinct correct implementation rises from
\claim{MechanismSftDominantMass}\% to
\claim{MechanismGrpoDominantMass}\%, while supervised samples already contain a
candidate at least as fast as the optimized conditional mean on
\claim{MechanismSupportCount} designs.  Finally, a bounded trajectory audit
shows genuine early hardware improvement followed by late proxy inflation and
falling equal-sample performance.  Correctness-gated optimization therefore
changes the one-draw distribution toward fast RTL, but real EDA remains the
reporting authority.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
RTL generation, reinforcement learning, large language models, FPGA,
design space exploration, reward hacking
\end{IEEEkeywords}
